thread.title: Qualcomm V. What Does China Want from Them?

author: Tiernan Ray
title: Qualcomm V. What Does China Want from Them?
text:
What does China want from the battle between Qualcomm ( QCOM ) and Broadcom ( AVGO )?
That’s a question some analysts are asking today as the Street responds to a sudden cancellation of Qualcomm’s annual meeting, and a fresh round of rhetoric between the two.
An interesting question, given petitioning by U.S. congressmen last week made it sound like Broadcom’s bid for Qualcomm is some sort of back-door plot by China to humble the U.S.
To recap: Qualcomm today confirmed reports out overnight that it is postponing its annual shareholder meeting , original scheduled fore tomorrow, after the government said the CFIUS organization, run by the Treasury Department, would review Broadcom’s hostile bid for Qualcomm, an unusual move before any deal is even agreed to.
Qualcomm took the chance to accuse Broadcom of “trivializing” national security; that came after Broadcom this morning accused Qualcomm of acting out of desperation, by filing a request “secretly” back in January for CFIUS review, and not telling Broadcom.
Broadcom fired another round this afternoon, repeating its claim it knew nothing of the CFIUS matter until yesterday, accusing Qualcomm of a lapse in disclosure to its shareholders.
Among those responding today, Cowen & Co .’s Karl Ackerman , who has an Outperform rating on Broadcom shares, implies President Donald Trump ’s decision last week to impose tariffs on some imports, including Chinese exports of steel, could complicate matters for Qualcomm.
That is because Qualcomm is still seeking approval for its bid to buy NXP Semiconductors ( NXPI ), which it intimated over a year ago. That means getting regulatory approval from Chinese regulators. Would they hold thinks up because of the new protectionist turn?
"Relative to QCOM/NXPI, which remains held-up by one final regulatory approval – MOFCOM, we wouldn’t completely rule out Trump’s protective trade rhetoric having unforeseen consequences to the elongation of MOFCOM’s approval process (certainly more so than MRVL/CAVM),” writes Ackerman, referring to China’s main regulatory body, MOFCOM .
As for Broadcom and Qualcomm, it all comes down to the vote by shareholders, now delayed, on Broadcom’s six nominees to Qualcomm’s board.
Whenever that happens — there is an initial postponement of up to 30 days — "If QCOM shareholders vote for the deal,” writes Ackerman, "then we think QCOM’s BoD must actively engage with AVGO, which would put a merger agreement between AVGO/QCOM in play."
Also weighing in today is Rosenblatt ’s Jun Zhang , who has a Neutral rating on Qualcomm stock. He thinks the Chinese really want Qualcomm independent — or, at least, Chinese smartphone makers chums as Oppo and Vivo , who use Qualcomm chips.
Why is that? Because a combined Broadcom and Qualcomm might resolve its relationship with Apple ( AAPL ), which would in turn make Qualcomm a less-responsive supplier to the smaller Chinese brands:
We believe Chinese smartphone OEMs have grown more concerned re- garding the pending Broadcom (AVGO: Buy) acquisition of Qualcomm. We believe that the second tier Chinese smartphone OEMs fear Broadcom could focus more on Apple, Samsung (005930-KR:NE) and Huawei in- creasing pricing pressure. Consequently, we believe many Chinese OEMs could join Qualcomm in fighting against the takeover. Additionally, we note many Chinese smartphone OEMs have signed framework contracts with Qualcomm to support Qualcomm’s RF business over the next 2-3 years.
Qualcomm stock today closed down 73 cents, or 1%, at $64.01, while Broadcom shares closed down $3.89, or 1.6%, at $246.98.
